title: Biology
summary: Cell and genetics, human body systems, vitamins and minerals, diseases with pathogens, vectors and vaccines, plant physiology and classification, and branches of biology with ecology. Biology is the most-asked science area in CGL GA — mostly direct one-line facts.

subtopics.title: Cell, organelles and genetics
subtopics.concept: The cell is the basic unit of life. Each organelle inside it has one job and one nickname, such as mitochondria as the powerhouse. Cells divide by mitosis for growth and by meiosis to make gametes. Genetics adds a few names and numbers: Mendel, Watson and Crick, and 46 human chromosomes.

tricks.title: Organelle nicknames: Power-Mito, Suicide-Lyso, Protein-Ribo, Packing-Golgi
tricks.body: These four nicknames answer most organelle questions.

example.q: Which organelle is called the 'suicide bag' of the cell?
steps: Suicide points to self-digestion.
Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes.

tricks.title: Cell discoverers in order
tricks.body: Hooke saw the cell (1665, dead cork). Leeuwenhoek saw it alive. Brown saw the nucleus. Schleiden and Schwann made the theory. Virchow said cells come from cells.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Leeuwenhoek discovered the cell.
mistakes.right: Hooke named the cell. Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.

mistakes.wrong: Saying the mother decides the child's sex.
mistakes.right: The father decides it. His sperm carries X or Y.

mistakes.wrong: Giving animal cells a cell wall.
mistakes.right: Only plants, fungi and bacteria have one.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking meiosis makes two identical cells.
mistakes.right: Mitosis gives 2 identical cells. Meiosis gives 4 cells with half the chromosomes.

mistakes.wrong: Saying every cell has a nucleus.
mistakes.right: Prokaryotes have none. Mature mammalian RBCs have none.

subtopics.notes:
### Who found what about the cell
Each scientist has one signature fact. Match the fact to the name.

| Discovery | Scientist |
|---|---|
| Cell (in cork, 1665) | **Robert Hooke** |
| First living cells, bacteria (single-lens microscope) | **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** |
| **Nucleus** (1831) | **Robert Brown** |
| **Cell theory** | **Schleiden** (plants) and **Schwann** (animals) |
| 'Omnis cellula e cellula': new cells come from existing cells | **Rudolf Virchow** |

> **Watch:** Hooke saw dead cork walls and named the cell. Leeuwenhoek was the first to see living cells.

### Cell organelles
An organelle is a small working part inside the cell.

| Organelle | Job or nickname |
|---|---|
| **Mitochondria** | **Powerhouse of the cell**. Aerobic respiration, ATP. Has its own DNA |
| **Ribosomes** | **Protein synthesis**. No membrane |
| **Lysosomes** | **'Suicide bags'**. Hold digestive enzymes |
| **Golgi apparatus** | Packaging and secretion |
| **Endoplasmic reticulum** | Transport. Rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins. Smooth ER makes lipids |
| **Chloroplast** | **Photosynthesis**. Plants only. Has its own DNA |
| **Nucleus** | Control centre. Holds the chromosomes (DNA) |
| **Vacuole** | Storage. Large in plant cells |
| **Cell wall** | Plants (**cellulose**) and fungi (**chitin**). Absent in animal cells |

> **Tip:** Four nicknames answer most questions: mitochondria = power, lysosome = suicide bag, ribosome = protein, Golgi = packing.

### Cell types and cell records
- **Prokaryotes** (bacteria, blue-green algae) have **no nuclear membrane** and no membrane-bound organelles.
- **Eukaryotes** have a true nucleus.
- Largest cell: **ostrich egg**. Longest cell: **nerve cell (neuron)**. Smallest cell: **Mycoplasma (PPLO)**.
- The ovum is the largest human cell.
- Mature mammalian **RBCs have no nucleus**. An RBC lives about 120 days. The spleen removes worn-out RBCs.

### Cell division
| | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Body growth and repair | Makes **gametes** |
| Cells formed | **2 identical** cells | 4 cells |
| Chromosome number | Stays the same | Halved |

Take a human cell. Mitosis keeps 46. Meiosis gives 23 in each gamete.

### Genetics basics
- **Gregor Mendel** is the **father of genetics**. He worked on the **garden pea** (Pisum sativum).
- His laws are dominance, segregation and independent assortment.
- **DNA double helix**: **Watson and Crick (1953)**, using X-ray data of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.
- DNA bases are A, T, G, C. RNA has **uracil** in place of thymine.

### Human chromosomes and inheritance
Body cells hold **46 chromosomes (23 pairs)**. That is 22 pairs of autosomes plus 1 pair of sex chromosomes. Gametes hold 23.

> **Rule:** The father decides the sex of the child. XX is female. XY is male.

- **Haemophilia** and **colour blindness** are **X-linked**. They are more common in males.
- **Down syndrome** is an extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21).

### Theories and names to know
- **Hugo de Vries**: mutation theory.
- **Darwin**: natural selection (*On the Origin of Species*, 1859).
- **Lamarck**: inheritance of acquired characters.
- **Har Gobind Khorana**: Nobel Prize 1968 for work on the genetic code.

patterns.name: Cell theory and discoverers
patterns.howToSpot: Words like 'who discovered the cell / nucleus / living cells', 'cell theory', 'omnis cellula e cellula', or a year (1665, 1831).
steps: Read the noun: cell, living cell, nucleus or theory.
Match it to its one scientist from the table.
Use the year to break ties: 1665 Hooke, 1831 Brown.
patterns.why: Each scientist has exactly one signature fact.

example.q: The cell theory was proposed by which pair of scientists?
steps: Theory means Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals).
Hooke only named the cell.
Virchow added that cells come from cells.

patterns.name: Organelle and its function or nickname
patterns.howToSpot: 'Powerhouse of the cell', 'suicide bags', 'which organelle makes protein', 'which organelle has its own DNA'.
steps: Find the nickname or job in the question.
Recall the pair from the organelle table.
For own DNA, choose mitochondria or chloroplast.
patterns.why: The question is always one nickname or one job.

example.q: Which organelle is called the 'suicide bag' of the cell?
steps: Suicide bag means it digests the cell itself.
Lysosomes hold digestive enzymes.

patterns.name: Prokaryote vs eukaryote, plant vs animal cell
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a prokaryote', 'no true nucleus', 'cell wall is made of', 'absent in animal cells'.
steps: Bacteria and blue-green algae are prokaryotes. Everything else is eukaryote.
Cell wall, chloroplast and large vacuole mark plant cells.
For 'absent in animal cells', pick cell wall or chloroplast.
patterns.why: Prokaryotes lack a nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles.

example.q: The cell wall of a plant cell is made of what?
steps: Plants use cellulose in the wall.
Fungi use chitin.

patterns.name: Cell division and chromosome numbers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Chromosomes in a human body cell', 'chromosomes in a gamete', 'mitosis vs meiosis', 'which division keeps the number the same'.
steps: Body cell: 46. Gamete: 23.
Growth and repair means mitosis: the number stays.
Gamete formation means meiosis: the number halves.
patterns.why: Meiosis halves the number so fertilisation can restore it.

example.q: A human gamete contains how many chromosomes?
steps: A body cell has 46.
Meiosis halves it: 46 / 2 = 23.

patterns.name: Genetics: Mendel, DNA and inheritance
patterns.howToSpot: 'Father of genetics', 'DNA double helix', 'Mendel worked on which plant', 'who decides the sex of a child'.
steps: Match the name to its one fact.
Mendel is the garden pea. Watson and Crick is 1953.
Sex: the mother always gives X. The father gives X or Y.
patterns.why: One name, one organism and one year make up the whole question.

example.q: Watson and Crick are famous for which work?
steps: Their year is 1953.
They built the model of DNA.

patterns.name: Blood cells and cell records
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which blood cells lack a nucleus', 'lifespan of RBC', 'largest / longest cell', 'which cell carries oxygen'.
steps: RBC has no nucleus, carries oxygen and lives about 120 days.
WBC defends. Platelets clot the blood.
Records: ovum is the largest human cell. Nerve cell is the longest.
patterns.why: Each blood cell has one job.

example.q: What is the average lifespan of a human red blood cell?
steps: RBCs live about 120 days.
The spleen removes worn-out RBCs.

revision: Hooke 1665 cork; Leeuwenhoek living cells; Brown nucleus 1831; Schleiden-Schwann theory; Virchow: cells from cells.
Mitochondria: powerhouse. Lysosome: suicide bag. Ribosome: protein. Golgi: packaging.
Cell wall: cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi. Absent in animal cells.
Largest cell: ostrich egg. Longest: neuron. Smallest: Mycoplasma.
Mitosis: 2 identical cells. Meiosis: gametes, chromosomes halved.
Human: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Gamete: 23. Father decides sex.
Mendel: pea. Watson and Crick: DNA 1953. Down syndrome: trisomy 21.

subtopics.title: Human body — organs, blood, digestion, glands
subtopics.concept: This subtopic is a list of standard facts: body records, blood and heart, digestion, hormones and the brain. Learn each fact as a pair, such as bile and liver or insulin and pancreas. A few numbers (206 bones, 37 °C, 120/80) are asked again and again.

formulas.name: Body mass index
formulas.note: Mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. 18.5–24.9 is the normal range (WHO)

tricks.title: Blood group giving: O gives, AB takes
tricks.body: O has no A or B antigens, so it can give to all. AB has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so it can take from all.

example.q: The universal recipient blood group is?
steps: AB has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.
So it accepts blood from all groups.

tricks.title: Brain parts: Cerebrum thinks, Cerebellum balances, Medulla keeps you alive
tricks.body: Thinking and memory: cerebrum. Balance and posture: cerebellum. Heartbeat and breathing: medulla oblongata.

mistakes.wrong: Saying bile contains digestive enzymes.
mistakes.right: Bile has no enzymes. It only emulsifies fats.

mistakes.wrong: Answering thyroid for the master gland.
mistakes.right: The master gland is the pituitary.

mistakes.wrong: Naming the heart or liver as the largest organ.
mistakes.right: Skin is the largest organ. The liver is the largest gland and internal organ.

mistakes.wrong: Answering liver for the largest endocrine gland.
mistakes.right: The largest endocrine gland is the thyroid.

mistakes.wrong: Saying bile is made in the gall bladder.
mistakes.right: The liver makes bile. The gall bladder only stores it.

subtopics.notes:
### Body records
These records are asked in almost every paper.

| Record | Answer |
|---|---|
| Largest organ | **Skin** |
| Largest gland / largest internal organ | **Liver** |
| Largest endocrine gland | **Thyroid** |
| Longest bone | **Femur** (thigh) |
| Smallest bone | **Stapes** (middle ear) |
| Smallest muscle | **Stapedius** (ear) |
| Strongest muscle (by force) | **Jaw (masseter)** |
| Bones in an adult | **206** |
| Bones in a newborn | about **300** (many fuse later) |
| Ribs | **12 pairs = 24** |
| Normal body temperature | **37 °C (98.6 °F)** |

> **Watch:** Largest gland is the liver. Largest endocrine gland is the thyroid. Do not mix the two.

### Blood and circulation
An adult has about 5 litres of blood. It has four parts.

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| **Plasma** (55%) | The liquid part |
| **RBC** | Carries oxygen on haemoglobin |
| **WBC** | Defence |
| **Platelets** | Clotting |

- **Blood groups**: ABO plus Rh. **O− is the universal donor. AB+ is the universal recipient.**
- The **heart** has 4 chambers: 2 atria and 2 ventricles.
- Its natural **pace-maker is the SA node**.
- Humans have **double circulation**. Blood passes through the heart twice per loop.
- A **sphygmomanometer** measures blood pressure. Normal is about **120/80 mm Hg**.
- A resting heart beats about **72 times a minute**.

> **Example:** In one day the heart beats $72 \times 60 \times 24 = 103{,}680$ times. That is about 1 lakh beats.

### Digestive system, organ by organ
| Organ | What it does |
|---|---|
| Mouth | **Salivary amylase** starts starch digestion |
| Stomach | **HCl** and **pepsin** (protein). A mucous lining protects the stomach |
| Liver | Makes **bile**. The gall bladder stores it |
| Pancreas | Sends **trypsin** (protein) and **lipase** (fat) |
| Small intestine | Final digestion and absorption (villi) |
| Large intestine | Absorbs only water |

> **Rule:** Bile has **no enzymes**. It only **emulsifies fat**, which means it breaks fat into tiny drops.

### Endocrine glands and hormones
A hormone is a chemical messenger made by a gland.

| Gland | Hormone and effect |
|---|---|
| **Pituitary** | 'Master gland'. Growth hormone. Too little gives dwarfism, too much gives gigantism |
| **Thyroid** | **Thyroxine** (contains iodine). Deficiency causes **goitre** |
| **Pancreas** | **Insulin** (from the islets of Langerhans) controls blood sugar. Failure is **diabetes** |
| **Adrenal** | Adrenaline, the 'fight-or-flight' hormone |
| Testes / ovaries | Testosterone / estrogen |

### Excretion and the brain
- **Kidneys** filter the blood. Each has about a million **nephrons**.
- Urine holds urea, water and salts. It reaches the bladder.
- **Cerebrum**: thinking. It is the largest part of the brain.
- **Cerebellum**: balance and posture.
- **Medulla oblongata**: involuntary heartbeat and breathing. A spine injury there is fatal.
- The **spinal cord** handles reflex actions without waiting for the brain.

### Body numbers
Body mass index (BMI) tells if weight suits height.

$$\text{BMI} = \dfrac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\text{height (m)}^{2}}$$

The normal range is 18.5 to 24.9 (WHO). Take 54 kg and 1.5 m. Then $\dfrac{54}{1.5^{2}} = 24$, which is normal.

> **Tip:** Convert 37 °C to Fahrenheit with $F = \dfrac{9C}{5} + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = 98.6$.

patterns.name: Organ and its secretion or function
patterns.howToSpot: 'Insulin is secreted by', 'bile is produced in', 'which organ filters the blood', 'HCl is secreted in'.
steps: Split the question: made where, stored where.
Use the digestive table for enzymes.
Use the brain list for cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla.
patterns.why: Making and storing are different: the liver makes bile, the gall bladder stores it.

steps: Bile is made in the largest gland.

patterns.why: Gland, hormone and disease form a fixed triangle.

example.q: Which gland is called the master gland?
steps: Its hormones steer the other glands.
Growth hormone comes from it.

patterns.name: Digestion steps and enzymes
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which enzyme digests protein / starch / fat', 'where is food absorbed', 'function of bile'.
steps: Amylase acts on starch. Pepsin and trypsin act on protein. Lipase acts on fat.
The small intestine does final digestion and absorption.
The large intestine takes only water.
patterns.why: Each enzyme works on one food type.

example.q: Digested food is absorbed mainly in which organ?
steps: Villi increase the surface area.
They line the small intestine.

patterns.name: Body numbers (computed)
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many times does the heart beat in a day', 'normal body temperature in °F', 'how much blood does an adult have'.
steps: Write the given rate, such as 72 a minute.
Multiply by 60 and by 24 for a day.
For temperature use F = 9C/5 + 32.
patterns.why: Split the multiplication into easy steps.

example.q: At 72 beats per minute, about how many times does the heart beat in a day?
steps: 72 × 60 = 4,320 beats an hour.

revision: 206 adult bones. Stapes smallest. Femur longest. Skin largest organ. Liver largest gland.
O− universal donor. AB+ universal recipient. SA node is the pace-maker.

Bile: no enzymes, emulsifies fat. Stomach: HCl and pepsin. Villi absorb in the small intestine.
Pituitary: master gland. Thyroxine needs iodine. Insulin from pancreas. Adrenaline: fight-or-flight.
Cerebrum thinks, cerebellum balances, medulla keeps the heart beating.
Body temperature 37 °C = 98.6 °F.

subtopics.title: Vitamins, minerals and nutrition
subtopics.concept: Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts. Lack of each one causes a named disease. Most questions ask for the pair: the vitamin and its disease, or the mineral and its problem. A few energy numbers (4, 4 and 9 kcal per gram) come with them.

tricks.title: Fat-soluble vitamins: KADE (or ADEK)
tricks.body: A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and are stored in the body. B and C dissolve in water.

tricks.title: Deficiency pairs: A-Andha (night blind), B1-Beriberi, C-sCurvy, D-Deformed bones (rickets), K-Klotting
tricks.body: Add B3 with Pellagra ('3 D's) and B12 with Pernicious anaemia (cobalt).

example.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes beriberi?
steps: Beriberi starts with B.
It goes with thiamine.

mistakes.wrong: Linking scurvy to vitamin D.
mistakes.right: Scurvy is vitamin C. Rickets is vitamin D.

mistakes.wrong: Calling vitamin C fat-soluble.
mistakes.right: It is water-soluble and cooking heat destroys it.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up kwashiorkor and marasmus.
mistakes.right: Kwashiorkor lacks protein only. Marasmus lacks protein and calories.

mistakes.wrong: Saying fat gives 4 kcal per gram.
mistakes.right: Fat gives 9 kcal per gram. Carbohydrate and protein give 4.

mistakes.wrong: Treating fluorine as harmless in large amounts.
mistakes.right: Too much fluorine causes fluorosis. Too little causes caries.

subtopics.notes:
### Vitamin and its deficiency disease
This table is the most asked table in the topic.

| Vitamin | Chemical name | Deficiency disease | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Retinol | **Night blindness**, xerophthalmia | Carrot, papaya, milk |
| **B₁** | Thiamine | **Beriberi** | Whole grains, pulses |
| **B₂** | Riboflavin | Cheilosis (cracked lips) | Milk, eggs |
| **B₃** | Niacin | **Pellagra** (3 Ds) | Groundnut |
| **B₁₂** | Cyanocobalamin | **Pernicious anaemia** | Meat, milk |
| **C** | Ascorbic acid | **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) | Amla, citrus |
| **D** | Calciferol | **Rickets** (children), osteomalacia (adults) | Sunlight, fish oil |
| **E** | Tocopherol | Sterility | Wheat germ |
| **K** | Phylloquinone | **Poor clotting** | Green leafy vegetables |

> **Tip:** Scurvy is C. Rickets is D. These two are the usual swaps in wrong-pair questions.

### Fat-soluble and water-soluble
- **Fat-soluble**: **A, D, E, K**. The body stores them, so too much can harm.
- **Water-soluble**: **B-complex and C**. They wash out daily.
- **Casimir Funk (1912)** coined the word 'vitamine'.
- Sunlight on the skin makes **vitamin D**.
- Cooking destroys vitamin C most easily.

### Minerals and their role
| Mineral | Role or deficiency |
|---|---|
| **Iron** | **Anaemia** (haemoglobin is iron-based) |
| **Iodine** | **Goitre** (thyroxine) |
| **Calcium** | Weak bones and teeth |
| **Phosphorus** | Bones and ATP |
| **Fluorine** | Too little causes dental caries. Too much causes **fluorosis** |
| **Sodium, potassium** | Nerve and muscle function |
| Zinc | Wound healing and immunity |

> **Watch:** Fluorine harms in both directions: too little and too much.

### Malnutrition: the two classics
| | Kwashiorkor | Marasmus |
|---|---|---|
| Lacks | Protein (calories are adequate) | Protein **and** calories |
| Look | Swollen belly, oedema, thin limbs | All skin and bones |
| Age | 1 to 3 years | Under one year |

> **Rule:** Kwashiorkor is swollen. Marasmus is shrunken.

Obesity is the opposite imbalance. **Roughage** (fibre) prevents constipation.

### Food energy
| Component | Energy |
|---|---|
| Carbohydrate | **4 kcal/g** |
| Protein | **4 kcal/g** |
| Fat | **9 kcal/g** |

Fat gives more than twice the energy per gram. A **30 g** fat snack gives $30 \times 9 = 270$ kcal.

> **Example:** A snack has 20 g fat and 10 g carbohydrate. Energy is $20 \times 9 + 10 \times 4 = 180 + 40 = 220$ kcal.

A balanced diet splits the calories roughly into 60% carbohydrates, 25 to 30% fat and 10 to 15% protein. **Basal metabolic rate (BMR)** is the energy burnt at rest. An adult needs about 2,000 to 2,500 kcal a day.

patterns.howToSpot: 'Scurvy is caused by deficiency of', 'rickets', 'beriberi', 'night blindness', 'pernicious anaemia'.
steps: Read the disease name.
Find it in the vitamin table.
Check D with rickets and C with scurvy first.
patterns.why: The pairs are fixed, so no reasoning is needed.

example.q: Pernicious anaemia is caused by the deficiency of which vitamin?
steps: Pernicious anaemia goes with cobalt.
The vitamin is cyanocobalamin.

patterns.name: Vitamin sources and solubility
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which vitamins are fat-soluble', 'made in the skin by sunlight', 'rich source of vitamin C'.
steps: Fat-soluble means A, D, E, K.
Sunlight on skin makes vitamin D.
Cooking destroys vitamin C the most.
patterns.why: The body stores fat-soluble vitamins and washes out the rest.

example.q: Which set contains only fat-soluble vitamins?
steps: Recall the word KADE.
The set is A, D, E, K.

patterns.name: Mineral and deficiency or role
patterns.howToSpot: 'Goitre is due to deficiency of', 'anaemia is caused by lack of', 'which mineral builds bones and teeth'.
steps: Iron gives anaemia.
Iodine gives goitre.
Calcium and phosphorus build bones and teeth.
patterns.why: Each mineral has one headline role.

example.q: Anaemia (low haemoglobin) most commonly results from deficiency of which mineral?
steps: Haemoglobin is an iron pigment.
Less iron means less oxygen carried.

patterns.name: Malnutrition: kwashiorkor vs marasmus
patterns.howToSpot: 'Kwashiorkor is caused by', 'swollen belly disease of children', 'difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus'.
steps: Swollen belly and oedema means kwashiorkor.
Skin and bones means marasmus.
Kwashiorkor lacks protein. Marasmus lacks protein and calories.
patterns.why: Swollen against shrunken separates the two.

example.q: A child with a swollen belly but adequate calorie intake suffers from what?
steps: The swelling is oedema.
Only protein is lacking.

patterns.name: Food energy values (computed)
patterns.howToSpot: 'How much energy does 1 g of fat give', a snack's total calories from given grams.
steps: Recall: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal per gram.
Multiply each part by its value.
Add the parts.
patterns.why: Fat gives the most energy per gram.

example.q: A snack has 25 g carbohydrate, 10 g protein and 10 g fat. What is its energy?
steps: Carbohydrate: 25 × 4 = 100.
Protein: 10 × 4 = 40.

patterns.name: Vitamin history and chemical names
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who coined the word vitamin', 'which vitamin is ascorbic acid', chemical names of vitamins.
steps: Casimir Funk coined 'vitamine' in 1912.
Match the chemical name from the table.
Ascorbic acid means scurvy means vitamin C.
patterns.why: The chemical name is often a giveaway for the disease.

example.q: The word 'vitamine' was coined by whom?
steps: He coined it in 1912.
His name is Casimir Funk.

revision: A night blindness, B₁ beriberi, B₃ pellagra, B₁₂ pernicious anaemia, C scurvy, D rickets, E sterility, K clotting.
Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K. Water-soluble: B and C.
'Vitamine' was coined by Casimir Funk. Vitamin D comes from sunlight.
Iron gives anaemia, iodine gives goitre, calcium gives bones, fluorine gives caries or fluorosis.
Kwashiorkor: protein lack, swollen. Marasmus: protein and calories lack, shrunken.
Energy: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal per gram.

subtopics.title: Diseases, pathogens, vectors and vaccines
subtopics.concept: Every common disease belongs to one pathogen type: bacteria, virus, protozoa or fungus. Many are carried by one named vector, such as a mosquito or fly. Add the vaccine and the scientist who found it, and most questions are covered.

tricks.title: Bacterial diseases: TB, Cholera, Typhoid, Diphtheria, Tetanus, Leprosy, Plague, Pertussis
tricks.body: A disease in this list is bacterial. Polio, measles, AIDS, dengue, rabies, chickenpox and hepatitis are viral. Malaria and kala-azar are protozoan.

example.q: Which of these is a viral disease: typhoid, cholera, measles, tetanus?
steps: Typhoid, cholera and tetanus are bacterial.
Measles is on the viral list.

tricks.title: Mosquito map: Anopheles-Malaria, Aedes-Dengue, Culex-Filaria
tricks.body: Aedes also spreads chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika (day-biting). Only the female mosquito bites for blood.

mistakes.wrong: Calling malaria a bacterial or viral disease.
mistakes.right: Malaria is protozoan (Plasmodium).

mistakes.wrong: Crediting Pasteur with the smallpox vaccine.
mistakes.right: Jenner made it. Pasteur made the rabies vaccine.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking antibiotics cure viral infections.
mistakes.right: Antibiotics act only on bacteria.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking ringworm is caused by a worm.
mistakes.right: Ringworm is a fungal infection.

mistakes.wrong: Saying mosquitoes spread AIDS.
mistakes.right: AIDS spreads only by blood, unsafe sex and shared needles.

subtopics.notes:
### Disease and pathogen type
A pathogen is a germ that causes disease. Sort each disease into its group first.

| Type | Diseases |
|---|---|
| **Bacteria** | **TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, leprosy, plague, whooping cough, anthrax** |
| **Virus** | **Dengue, chikungunya, rabies, polio, measles, mumps, AIDS, COVID-19, smallpox, influenza, jaundice (hepatitis)** |
| **Protozoa** | **Malaria, kala-azar, amoebiasis (dysentery), sleeping sickness** |
| **Fungus** | **Ringworm, athlete's foot** |

> **Tip:** The bacterial six are cholera, typhoid, TB, tetanus, leprosy and plague. The viral five are dengue, rabies, polio, measles and AIDS.

### Vectors: who carries what
A vector is a living carrier of a pathogen.

| Vector | Disease |
|---|---|
| **Female Anopheles** | **Malaria** (Plasmodium) |
| **Aedes aegypti** | **Dengue, chikungunya, zika** |
| **Culex** | **Filariasis or elephantiasis** (Wuchereria bancrofti) |
| **Sandfly** | **Kala-azar** (Leishmania) |
| **Tsetse fly** | **Sleeping sickness** (Trypanosoma) |
| **Rat flea** | **Plague** |

Only the female mosquito bites.

> **Watch:** AIDS is never spread by mosquitoes. It spreads only by blood, unsafe sex and shared needles.

### Vaccines, antibiotics and discoverers
| Scientist | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Edward Jenner** | First **vaccine**: smallpox, 1796. 'Vaccine' comes from 'vacca', cow |
| **Louis Pasteur** | Germ theory, pasteurisation, **rabies vaccine** |
| **Robert Koch** | **TB bacterium** (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), also anthrax and cholera |
| **Alexander Fleming** | **Penicillin, 1928**, the first antibiotic (mould *Penicillium notatum*) |
| Florey and Chain | Made penicillin into a medicine |
| **Banting and Best (1921)** | **Insulin** for diabetes |
| **Ronald Ross** | Proved mosquitoes carry malaria (worked in India, Nobel 1902) |
| **Joseph Lister** | **Antiseptic surgery** (carbolic acid) |

### Key numbers and controls
- Smallpox was the first disease **eradicated**. WHO declared it in **1980**.
- **BCG** vaccine protects against TB. **MMR** covers measles, mumps and rubella.
- Polio drops belong to the **Pulse Polio** campaign.
- Cholera, typhoid and jaundice spread through contaminated **water and food**.
- Safe drinking water and vaccination are the cheapest shields.

### Scale words
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Endemic** | Always present in a local area |
| **Epidemic** | Outbreak in a region |
| **Pandemic** | Worldwide outbreak (COVID-19) |

### Blood values and disorders
- Normal haemoglobin is about **12 to 16 g/dL**. Low haemoglobin is **anaemia**.
- Normal RBC count is about 5 million per mm³. WBC is about 6,000 to 8,000 per mm³.
- An RBC lives about 120 days.
- **Thalassaemia** and **sickle-cell anaemia** are genetic blood disorders. They do not spread from person to person.

> **Note:** Antibiotics act only on bacteria. They do not cure viral infections.

subtopics.notes:
### Classification: the ladder
**Carolus Linnaeus** is the **father of taxonomy**. He gave **binomial nomenclature**, a two-word scientific name of genus plus species, written in italics. Example: *Mangifera indica*.

**R.H. Whittaker (1969)** gave the **five-kingdom** system.

1. **Monera**
2. **Protista**
3. **Fungi**
4. **Plantae**
5. **Animalia**

Earlier systems used two kingdoms: plants and animals.

Plants divide into two big groups.

| Group | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Cryptogams** | Seedless | Algae, fungi, bryophytes, pteridophytes |
| **Phanerogams** | Seed plants | Gymnosperms (naked seed), angiosperms (seed inside fruit) |

### Monocot and dicot
| | Monocot | Dicot |
|---|---|---|
| Seed leaves | One | Two |
| Leaf veins | **Parallel** | **Reticulate** (net-like) |
| Roots | Fibrous | Taproot |
| Examples | Wheat, rice, maize | Mango, pea, gram |

> **Tip:** Parallel veins mean monocot. Net-like veins mean dicot.

### Plant hormones
| Hormone | Job |
|---|---|
| **Auxin** | Cell elongation. Bending to light (**phototropism**) |
| **Gibberellin** | Stem elongation. Seed germination |
| **Cytokinin** | Cell division. Delays leaf ageing |
| **Ethylene** (gas) | **Fruit ripening** |
| **Abscisic acid** | Stress hormone. Closes stomata. Promotes wilting and dormancy |

### Photosynthesis and transport
Photosynthesis happens in the **chloroplast**, which holds the green pigment **chlorophyll**. Sunlight drives it.

$$6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$$

> **Rule:** The oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.

- Leaves exchange gases through **stomata**.
- **Transpiration** pulls water up the xylem.
- Phloem carries food.
- Excess water vapour escapes mainly through the lower surface of the leaf.

### Edible parts of plants
| Plant | Edible part |
|---|---|
| Carrot, radish, beetroot, turnip | **Root** |
| Potato, ginger, turmeric, onion (bulb), sugarcane | **Stem (modified)** |
| Cabbage, spinach, lettuce | **Leaves** |
| Cauliflower, broccoli | **Flower** |
| Tomato, brinjal, pumpkin, cucumber | **Fruit** |
| Groundnut, gram, mustard, rice, wheat | **Seed** |
| Apple, cashew | Fleshy **thalamus** (accessory fruit) |

> **Watch:** Potato, ginger, turmeric and onion grow underground but are stems. Sweet potato is a true root.

### Reproduction and scientific names
Vegetative propagation uses runners and bulbs. People add **grafting, layering, cutting and tissue culture**. Wind pollinates maize and wheat, which have light dry pollen. Insects visit bright petals with nectar.

| Organism | Scientific name |
|---|---|
| Mango | *Mangifera indica* |
| Neem | *Azadirachta indica* |
| Banyan | *Ficus benghalensis* |
| Tamarind | *Tamarindus indica* |
| Potato | *Solanum tuberosum* |
| Rice | *Oryza sativa* |
| Tiger | *Panthera tigris* |
| Frog | *Rana tigrina* |

subtopics.notes:
### Branches of study
The word ending -ology means the study of. The front part tells you what.

| Branch | Studies |
|---|---|
| **Ornithology** | **Birds** |
| **Entomology** | **Insects** |
| **Ichthyology** | **Fishes** |
| **Herpetology** | **Reptiles and amphibians** |
| **Mycology** | **Fungi** |
| **Virology** | Viruses |
| **Cytology** | Cells |
| **Histology** | Tissues |
| **Oncology** | Cancer |
| **Cardiology** | Heart |
| **Ophthalmology** | Eye |
| **Anthology** | Flowers |

Apiology is bees. Malacology is molluscs.

> **Watch:** Entomology is insects. Etymology is the study of word origins.

### Culture words: rearing living things
| Word | Rears or grows |
|---|---|
| **Apiculture** | Honeybees (honey) |
| **Sericulture** | Silkworms (silk) |
| **Pisciculture** | Fish |
| **Aquaculture** | Water organisms |
| **Horticulture** | Garden plants |
| **Floriculture** | Flowers |
| **Vermiculture** | Earthworms |
| **Silviculture** | Forest trees |
| **Poultry** | Fowl |

> **Tip:** Decode the root: api is bee, seri is silk, pisci is fish, vermi is worm, silvi is forest.

### Colour revolutions in India
- **Green**: food grain. M.S. Swaminathan in India. Norman Borlaug worldwide.
- **White**: milk. **Verghese Kurien**, Operation Flood.
- **Blue**: fish.
- **Yellow**: oilseeds.

### Ecosystem and the 10% law
An **ecosystem** is a living community plus its physical surroundings.

The food chain runs in one direction.

1. **Producers** (green plants)
2. **Herbivores** (primary consumers)
3. **Carnivores** (secondary and tertiary consumers)

**Decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) recycle nutrients. A **food web** is many chains linked together.

> **Rule:** Lindeman's 10% law says only about 10% of energy passes to the next level.

$$E_n = E_1 \times (0.1)^{n-1}$$

Here $E_1$ is the producer energy and $n$ is the level. Take 10,000 J at the producers. The herbivores get 1,000 J. Small carnivores get 100 J. Big carnivores get 10 J.

Energy flows one way. Nutrients cycle. **Bioaccumulation** makes toxins build up along the chain.

### Cycles and conservation
- **Nitrogen cycle**: soil nitrogen goes to plants, then animals, then back to soil. **Rhizobium** bacteria in legume root nodules fix the nitrogen.
- The **carbon cycle** ties together respiration, photosynthesis and fuels.
- **Jim Corbett National Park (1936)** is India's first national park.
- **Project Tiger** began in 1973.
- The **Chipko movement (1973)**: villagers hugged trees to save them.
- The **IUCN Red List** ranks threatened species (extinct, vulnerable, least concern). The **Red Data Book** records them.
- Ramsar sites are wetlands.

### Pollution and milestones
- Air pollutants: CO, SO₂, NOₓ and particulates.
- **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand) measures water pollution. Higher BOD means dirtier water.
- ***Silent Spring*** (Rachel Carson, 1962) warned against pesticides like **DDT**.
- **Dolly the sheep (1996)** was the first cloned mammal.
- **Norman Borlaug** is the father of the Green Revolution.
- **Salim Ali** is the birdman of India.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Scurvy / rickets / goitre / anaemia is caused by deficiency of…', 'which vitamin is fat-soluble', kwashiorkor vs marasmus, wrong-pair questions on the vitamin table.
pyqPatterns.approach: Sing the ladder: A–night blindness, B₁–beriberi, B₃–pellagra, B₁₂–pernicious anaemia, C–scurvy, D–rickets, E–sterility, K–clotting. Fat-soluble = A, D, E, K. Minerals: iron–anaemia, iodine–goitre, calcium–bones. Kwashiorkor = protein lack (swollen), marasmus = protein + calories (shrunken).

example.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
example.solution: Scurvy — bleeding gums and slow healing. Sailors avoided it with citrus; amla is the richest Indian source.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Dengue / malaria / TB is caused by or spread by…', 'which of these is a viral disease', 'elephantiasis is transmitted by', odd-one-out among pathogens.
pyqPatterns.approach: Classify first: bacteria (TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, leprosy, plague), virus (dengue, rabies, polio, measles, AIDS), protozoa (malaria, kala-azar, amoebiasis), fungus (ringworm). Vectors: Anopheles–malaria, Aedes–dengue/chikungunya, Culex–elephantiasis, sandfly–kala-azar, tsetse–sleeping sickness, rat flea–plague. Dengue (viral) and malaria (protozoan) both ride mosquitoes but are different microbes — the favourite odd-one-out.

example.q: Which mosquito transmits dengue?
example.solution: Aedes aegypti — it bites by day and also carries chikungunya and zika. Malaria rides the female Anopheles instead.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Largest gland / largest organ / longest bone / smallest bone', 'universal blood donor', 'bile is produced in', 'pace-maker of the heart', 'how many bones in an adult'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Records: skin largest organ, liver largest gland, thyroid largest endocrine gland, femur longest bone, stapes smallest bone, 206 adult bones. Blood: O− universal donor, AB+ universal recipient, platelets clot, SA node pace-maker. Secretions: liver makes bile (gall bladder stores it, no enzymes), stomach HCl + pepsin, pancreas insulin + trypsin. Pituitary is the master gland; thyroxine needs iodine.

example.q: The smallest bone in the human body is:
example.solution: Stapes, in the middle ear. The largest gland is the liver and the longest bone the femur — keep the three records separate.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who discovered penicillin / the cell / the vaccine', 'insulin was discovered by', 'who proved mosquitoes carry malaria', match-the-column of biologists.
pyqPatterns.approach: Timeline table: Hooke–cell (1665), Leeuwenhoek–living cells, Brown–nucleus, Schleiden + Schwann–cell theory, Virchow–omnis cellula; Jenner–first vaccine (smallpox, 1796), Pasteur–rabies vaccine and pasteurisation, Koch–TB bacterium, Fleming–penicillin (1928), Banting & Best–insulin (1921), Ross–mosquito-malaria link, Mendel–genetics, Watson & Crick–DNA double helix.

example.q: Who discovered penicillin?
example.solution: Alexander Fleming, in 1928, from the mould Penicillium notatum. Koch identified the TB bacterium; Pasteur gave the rabies vaccine.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Powerhouse of the cell / suicide bags', 'which organelle makes protein', 'human body cell has how many chromosomes', 'sex of the child is determined by', 'Mendel worked on'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Nickname pairs: mitochondria–powerhouse, ribosome–protein factory, lysosome–suicide bag, Golgi–post office; mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA. Genetics: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), meiosis halves to 23 in gametes, XX female / XY male so the father decides sex; Mendel = father of genetics (pea plant), Watson & Crick = DNA double helix.

example.q: The sex of a child is determined by:
example.solution: The father's sperm — it carries either X (girl, XX) or Y (boy, XY); the mother's egg always gives X.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Ornithology / entomology / sericulture / apiculture is the study or rearing of', 'study of cancer', 'ichthyology', match-the-column of -ology words.
pyqPatterns.approach: Branches: ornithology–birds, entomology–insects (not etymology!), ichthyology–fish, herpetology–reptiles and amphibians, mycology–fungi, cytology–cells, oncology–cancer, cardiology–heart. Cultures: apiculture–bees, sericulture–silkworms, pisciculture–fish, vermiculture–earthworms, horticulture–gardens. Decode the Latin root when unsure (api-, seri-, pisci-).

example.q: Sericulture is associated with:
example.solution: Rearing silkworms for silk. Apiculture keeps bees, pisciculture farms fish — root + culture decodes each word.

pyqPatterns.approach: Hormones: auxin–elongation and phototropism, gibberellin–stem growth, cytokinin–cell division, ethylene–fruit ripening, abscisic acid–stress. Edible parts: carrot–root, potato/ginger/onion–stem, cabbage–leaf, cauliflower–flower, tomato–fruit, groundnut–seed. Classification: Linnaeus–binomial, Whittaker–5 kingdoms, bacteria in Monera; monocot one cotyledon + parallel veins, dicot two + reticulate; xylem water up, phloem food.

example.q: Which plant hormone is a gas that ripens fruit?
example.solution: Ethylene — a ripe banana releases it and ripens neighbouring fruit. Auxin bends shoots toward light; ABA closes stomata under stress.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The scientific name of mango / neem / rice / tiger', 'in binomial nomenclature the first word is', italics and capitalisation rules.
pyqPatterns.approach: Binomial = Genus (capital) + species (small), both italics. Mango Mangifera indica, neem Azadirachta indica, banyan Ficus benghalensis, tamarind Tamarindus indica, potato Solanum tuberosum, rice Oryza sativa, tiger Panthera tigris, frog Rana tigrina. Watch the two *-indica* pairings: mango and neem share the species name, not the genus.

example.q: In Mangifera indica, the word Mangifera denotes the:
example.solution: Genus — the first, capitalised word; indica is the species. The binomial system is Linnaeus's.

solvedExamples.solution: Vitamin C (**ascorbic acid**) is needed to make collagen; its deficiency causes **scurvy** — bleeding and swollen gums, slow wound healing. Rickets is vitamin D, beriberi is B1 and night blindness is A.

solvedExamples.q: Which blood group is known as the universal donor?
solvedExamples.solution: Group **O** red cells carry **no A or B antigens**, so they are not attacked by the recipient's anti-A or anti-B antibodies — **O is the universal donor** (strictly O negative). **AB** is the universal recipient.
Malaria is caused by the **protozoan *Plasmodium*** and spread by the bite of an infected **female Anopheles** mosquito. Ronald Ross proved the mosquito link (Nobel 1902).

solvedExamples.q: The edible part of the potato is a:
solvedExamples.solution: The potato is a **tuber — a modified underground stem**. Its 'eyes' are buds at nodes, which roots do not have. Sweet potato, by contrast, is a modified root.

practice.q: Which organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
practice.solution: **Mitochondria** carry out aerobic respiration and produce **ATP**, the cell's energy currency — hence 'powerhouse'. Ribosomes make proteins and lysosomes are the 'suicide bags'.

practice.q: Who first discovered the cell, in 1665?
practice.solution: **Robert Hooke** observed box-like compartments in a thin slice of **cork** in 1665 and called them 'cells'. Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831) and Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.

practice.q: In a food chain, producers trap 10,000 J of energy. According to the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
practice.solution: Only about **10%** passes to each next level: producers 10,000 J → primary consumers 1,000 J → **secondary consumers 100 J**.

practice.q: Which is the largest gland in the human body?
practice.solution: The **liver** is the largest gland (and largest internal organ). It secretes bile, stores glycogen and detoxifies substances. The pituitary is the 'master gland', not the largest.

practice.q: The smallest bone in the human body is:
practice.solution: The **stapes** (stirrup) in the **middle ear** is the smallest bone. The femur (thigh bone) is the longest. Malleus and incus are the other two ear ossicles, both larger than the stapes.

practice.q: Insulin is secreted by:
practice.solution: **Insulin** is secreted by the **β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas**. It lowers blood glucose; lack of it causes **diabetes mellitus**.

practice.q: Rickets in children is caused by deficiency of:
practice.solution: **Vitamin D (calciferol)** helps absorb calcium and phosphorus. Without it bones stay soft and bend — **rickets** in children, osteomalacia in adults. Sunlight lets the skin make vitamin D.

practice.q: Goitre is caused by deficiency of:
practice.solution: **Iodine** is needed to make **thyroxine**. When it is short, the thyroid gland enlarges — **goitre**. Iron deficiency causes anaemia.

practice.q: Vitamin K is essential for:
practice.solution: **Vitamin K** is needed to make clotting factors (such as prothrombin) in the liver; its deficiency leads to excessive bleeding. Vision needs vitamin A, gums need C, bones need D.

practice.q: Dengue fever is transmitted by which mosquito?
practice.solution: **Dengue** (a viral disease) is spread by the day-biting **Aedes** mosquito (*Aedes aegypti*), which also spreads chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever. Anopheles spreads malaria and Culex spreads filariasis.

practice.q: Penicillin, the first antibiotic, was discovered by:
practice.solution: **Alexander Fleming** discovered penicillin in **1928** from the mould *Penicillium notatum*. Jenner made the smallpox vaccine, Pasteur the rabies vaccine, and Koch discovered the TB bacterium.

practice.q: Tuberculosis is caused by a:
practice.solution: TB is caused by the bacterium ***Mycobacterium tuberculosis***, discovered by Robert Koch (1882). The **BCG** vaccine protects against it and the **Mantoux** test detects infection.

practice.q: Which plant hormone is responsible for the ripening of fruits?
practice.solution: **Ethylene**, a gaseous hormone, speeds up **fruit ripening**. Auxin controls cell elongation, cytokinin promotes cell division and gibberellin causes stem elongation.

practice.q: The five-kingdom classification of living organisms was proposed by:
practice.solution: **R.H. Whittaker** proposed the five kingdoms — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — in **1969**. Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature and the two-kingdom system.
practice.shortcut: My Pet Fish Plays Alone — Whittaker.

practice.q: Ornithology is the study of:
practice.solution: **Ornithology** is the study of **birds** (Greek *ornis*, bird). Insects — entomology, fish — ichthyology, fungi — mycology.

practice.q: Who first saw and named **'cells'** in cork (1665)?
practice.solution: **Robert Hooke**, in *Micrographia* (1665), saw box-like dead cork walls and named them cells. Leeuwenhoek later saw living cells.

practice.q: The **nucleus** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Robert Brown (1831)** found the nucleus inside orchid cells. Schleiden and Schwann built the cell theory; Virchow added 'cells from cells'.

practice.q: *Omnis cellula e cellula* (every cell from a pre-existing cell) was stated by —
practice.solution: **Virchow (1855)** completed the cell theory with this line. Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) had proposed the theory itself.

practice.q: The **'powerhouse of the cell'** is —
practice.solution: **Mitochondria** run respiration and make ATP — hence the powerhouse. They also carry their own DNA.

practice.q: **Protein synthesis** in a cell is done by —
practice.solution: **Ribosomes** are the 'protein factories'. Lysosomes digest; chloroplasts photosynthesise.

practice.q: Which organelles contain their **own DNA**, apart from the nucleus?
practice.solution: **Mitochondria and chloroplasts** are semi-autonomous — both keep their own circular DNA, a sign of their bacterial ancestors.

practice.q: Which structure is **absent in animal cells**?
practice.solution: A **cellulose cell wall** is plant-only (with chloroplasts and a big central vacuole). Animal cells have a centrosome instead.

practice.q: Which of these is a **prokaryote**?
practice.solution: **Bacteria** (and blue-green algae) have no true nucleus — prokaryotes. Amoeba, fungi and plants are eukaryotes.

practice.q: A normal **human body cell** contains how many chromosomes?
practice.solution: **46 chromosomes = 23 pairs**; 22 pairs are autosomes, the 23rd pair carries the sex chromosomes XX or XY.

practice.q: During **meiosis**, the chromosome number of a human cell —
practice.solution: **Meiosis** halves the number to make gametes (23); **mitosis** keeps 46 for growth. Fertilisation adds 23 + 23 back to 46.

practice.q: Who is called the **father of genetics**?
practice.solution: **Mendel**, an Austrian monk, deduced the laws of inheritance from garden-pea experiments. Darwin gave evolution; Watson and Crick, the DNA model.

practice.q: Mendel's experiments on heredity were performed on —
practice.solution: **Pisum sativum** — seven clear pairs of contrasting traits (tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled…). The fruit fly was Morgan's genetics workhorse later.

practice.q: The **sex of a child** is determined by —
practice.solution: The mother's egg always carries X; the father's sperm carries X (girl, XX) or Y (boy, XY) — so the **father determines sex**.

practice.q: The **double-helix model of DNA** was proposed by —
practice.solution: **James Watson and Francis Crick**, 1953. A gene is a segment of this DNA that codes one trait.

practice.q: The **largest cell** in the human body is —
practice.solution: The **ovum** is the largest; the **nerve cell** is the longest (up to about a metre). RBCs are among the smallest.

practice.q: Which blood cells **lack a nucleus** and carry oxygen?
practice.solution: Mature **RBCs** throw out their nucleus to pack in more **haemoglobin** (iron-based oxygen carrier). WBCs have nuclei and fight infection.

practice.q: The **largest gland** in the human body is —
practice.solution: **Liver** — largest gland and largest internal organ. The thyroid is only the largest ENDOCRINE gland.

practice.q: The **longest bone** in the human body is the —
practice.solution: **Femur** (thigh bone). The humerus is the upper arm; tibia and radius are lower leg and forearm bones.

practice.q: An adult human skeleton has how many bones?
practice.solution: **206** in an adult; a newborn starts near 300 and many fuse as it grows. Ribs add 12 pairs to the count.

practice.q: The **smallest muscle** in the human body is —
practice.solution: **Stapedius** in the middle ear moves the stapes bone. The masseter (jaw) is the strongest by force.

practice.q: The **universal donor** blood group is —
practice.solution: **O−** has no A, B or Rh antigens, so nobody's blood rejects it. AB+ is the universal recipient.

practice.q: Blood **clotting** is carried out by —
practice.solution: **Platelets (thrombocytes)** gather at a cut and trigger fibrin formation. WBC fight germs; RBC carry oxygen.

practice.q: The natural **pace-maker of the heart** is —
practice.solution: The **SA node** in the right atrium fires the beat — artificial pace-makers only replace it when it fails.

practice.q: Blood pressure is measured with a —
practice.solution: **Sphygmomanometer** — normal value 120/80 mm Hg (systolic/diastolic). A barometer measures air pressure.

practice.q: **Insulin**, which controls blood sugar, is secreted by the —
practice.solution: The **pancreas** (islets of Langerhans) secretes insulin; its shortage causes **diabetes**. The liver stores glycogen but makes no insulin.

practice.q: Bile is **stored** in the —
practice.solution: Made in the **liver**, stored in the **gall bladder**, released into the small intestine. Bile itself has no enzymes — it only emulsifies fat.

practice.q: The functional (filtering) unit of the **kidney** is the —
practice.solution: Each kidney packs about a million **nephrons**. Alveolus belongs to the lung, villus to the gut, neuron to nerves.

practice.q: Which part of the **brain** controls balance and posture?
practice.solution: **Cerebellum** — balance and coordinated movement. Cerebrum thinks; medulla runs heartbeat and breathing involuntarily.

practice.q: **Goitre**, a swelling of the neck, is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: Iodised salt prevents it. The **thyroid** needs iodine to make **thyroxine**; without it the gland swells working harder.

practice.q: **Adrenaline**, the 'fight-or-flight' hormone, is secreted by the —
practice.solution: **Adrenal glands** (on the kidneys) release adrenaline in emergencies — faster heartbeat, more blood sugar, instant energy.

practice.q: Over-secretion of **growth hormone** in children causes —
practice.solution: Too much growth hormone from the pituitary in childhood → **gigantism**; too little → dwarfism; in adults, acromegaly.

practice.q: Which enzyme in **saliva** starts digesting starch?
practice.solution: **Salivary amylase** breaks starch while you chew. Pepsin and trypsin take protein; lipase takes fat.

practice.q: The enzyme **pepsin**, active in the stomach, digests —
practice.solution: **Pepsin** needs the stomach's **HCl** (strong acid) to work on protein. Amylase handles starch and lipase fat.

practice.q: A person's heart beats at **72 per minute**. Roughly how many beats is that in a **day**?
practice.solution: 72 × 60 = 4,320 per hour; × 24 = **103,680** per day — about 1 lakh beats daily.

practice.q: Normal human body temperature of **37 °C** equals —
practice.solution: F = 9 × 37/5 + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = **98.6 °F** — the standard body-temperature pair.

practice.q: **Rickets** in children is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin D** (with calcium) hardens bones; its lack bends them — rickets. In adults the same lack gives osteomalacia.

practice.q: **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)** — sailors got scurvy on long voyages without fresh citrus. Amla is the richest Indian source.

practice.q: **Beriberi** results from the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **B₁ (thiamine)** — common where polished rice replaces whole grain. B₃ gives pellagra; B₂ cheilosis.

practice.q: **Night blindness** is an early sign of the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin A (retinol)** — carrots and papaya are rich sources; advanced lack causes xerophthalmia and corneal damage.

practice.q: **Pellagra** is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **B₃ (niacin)** — the '3 Ds': dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia (and death if untreated). Groundnut is a good source.

practice.q: **Vitamin K** deficiency mainly causes —
practice.solution: **K = Koagulation** — the liver needs it to make clotting factors. Green leafy vegetables supply it.

practice.q: Which group is **entirely fat-soluble**?
practice.solution: **A, D, E, K** — they store in fat and liver, so excess can be toxic. B-complex and C are water-soluble and need daily intake.

practice.q: Which vitamin is synthesised in the **skin** on exposure to sunlight?
practice.solution: UV light converts a skin sterol into **vitamin D** — the 'sunshine vitamin'. Deficiency gives rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults).

practice.q: The richest common Indian source of **vitamin C** is —
practice.solution: **Amla** tops the list (with guava close behind). Citrus fruits are famous but amla has several times more.

practice.q: **Goitre** is caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Iodine** is part of thyroxine; without it the thyroid swells. Iodised salt is the prevention.

practice.q: **Anaemia** is chiefly caused by the deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Iron** builds the haemoglobin that carries oxygen; low iron → pale, tired, breathless. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency gives the rarer pernicious anaemia.

practice.q: **Fluorosis** (mottling of teeth and bones) is caused by —
practice.solution: **Too much fluorine** in drinking water causes fluorosis; a little protects against dental caries — the dose makes the poison.

practice.q: **Kwashiorkor** is caused by the severe deficiency of —
practice.solution: **Protein deficiency** with enough calories — swollen belly and oedema in children aged 1–3. Marasmus lacks protein AND calories.

practice.q: **Marasmus** differs from kwashiorkor because in marasmus the child lacks —
practice.solution: **Marasmus = protein + calorie deficiency** — the infant is wasted, skin and bones, under a year old. Kwashiorkor children swell instead.

practice.q: Which nutrient gives the **maximum energy per gram**?
practice.solution: **Fat — 9 kcal/g**, more than double carbohydrate or protein. That is why the body stores spare energy as fat.

practice.q: A food packet contains **30 g carbohydrate** and **10 g protein**. Its total energy is —
practice.solution: Carb 30 × 4 = 120 kcal; protein 10 × 4 = 40 kcal; total = **160 kcal**. Had it been fat, each gram would count 9.

practice.q: The word **'vitamine'** was coined by —
practice.solution: **Casimir Funk (1912)** coined 'vitamine' while studying beriberi. Fleming discovered penicillin — a different hall of fame.

practice.q: **Ascorbic acid** is the chemical name of —
practice.solution: **Vitamin C = ascorbic acid**. Retinol–A, calciferol–D, tocopherol–E, thiamine–B₁, cyanocobalamin–B₁₂.

practice.q: **Tuberculosis** is caused by a —
practice.solution: **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** — a bacterium, identified by Robert Koch. BCG vaccination protects against it.

practice.q: Which of these is a **protozoan** disease?
practice.solution: **Malaria** — the parasite *Plasmodium* is a protozoan. Dengue is viral, TB bacterial, ringworm fungal.

practice.q: **Cholera** and **typhoid** are caused by —
practice.solution: Both are **bacterial**, water/food-borne: *Vibrio cholerae* and *Salmonella typhi* — the classic unsafe-water pair.

practice.q: **Dengue** is transmitted by the —
practice.solution: **Aedes aegypti** carries dengue (and chikungunya, zika) — it bites by day. Anopheles gives malaria.

practice.q: **Malaria** is spread by the bite of —
practice.solution: The **female Anopheles** injects *Plasmodium*; Ronald Ross proved the link in India. Only female mosquitoes bite.

practice.q: **Sleeping sickness** is transmitted by the —
practice.solution: The **tsetse fly** (African) carries *Trypanosoma*. The sandfly gives kala-azar; the rat flea, plague.

practice.q: **Kala-azar** (visceral leishmaniasis) is spread by the —
practice.solution: The **sandfly** carries the protozoan *Leishmania*. Fever with spleen enlargement is the signature.

practice.q: The **BCG vaccine** protects against —
practice.solution: **BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin)** — given at birth against TB. Polio drops and MMR cover the other diseases.

practice.q: The **first vaccine** ever developed was against —
practice.solution: **Edward Jenner, 1796**, against smallpox — from 'vacca' (cow) comes the word vaccine. Smallpox was also the first eradicated disease.

practice.q: The **MMR vaccine** protects against —
practice.solution: **MMR = measles, mumps, rubella** (German measles) — a live-virus shot given in childhood.

practice.q: **Penicillin** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Fleming, 1928** — noticed mould killing bacteria in a forgotten dish. Pasteur gave germ theory; Jenner, the first vaccine.

practice.q: The bacterium causing **tuberculosis** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Robert Koch** — the TB bacillus (1882), plus anthrax and cholera bacteria. Pasteur is the wider germ-theory man.

practice.q: **Insulin** was discovered by —
practice.solution: **Frederick Banting and Charles Best (1921)** isolated insulin — turning diabetes from a death sentence into a manageable condition.

practice.q: A disease outbreak restricted to one **region** is an —
practice.solution: **Epidemic** = regional outbreak; **pandemic** = worldwide (COVID-19); **endemic** = permanently local (malaria in some districts).

practice.q: **AIDS** is NOT transmitted by —
practice.solution: HIV travels in blood and body fluids — never by mosquito bite, touch or shared meals. The virus destroys helper T-cells.

practice.q: The average lifespan of a human **red blood cell** is —
practice.solution: **120 days** — the spleen then recycles them, hence its nickname 'graveyard of RBCs'.

practice.q: **Sickle-cell anaemia** is a —
practice.solution: It is **inherited** — a gene fault makes RBCs sickle-shaped, so they clog capillaries. Thalassaemia is the other famous genetic blood disorder.

practice.q: The **five-kingdom** classification was proposed by —
practice.solution: **Whittaker (1969)**: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Linnaeus gave binomial nomenclature.

practice.q: Who is called the **father of taxonomy**?
practice.solution: **Linnaeus** — he introduced binomial nomenclature (*Species Plantarum*, 1753): a two-word scientific name for every organism.

practice.q: In the five-kingdom system, **bacteria** belong to the kingdom —
practice.solution: **Monera** holds the prokaryotes — bacteria and blue-green algae. Protista is single-celled eukaryotes like Amoeba.

practice.q: The **potato** is a modified —
practice.solution: An underground **stem tuber** — the 'eyes' are buds. Sweet potato is the root; the two are the classic pair.

practice.q: **Carrot** is an example of an edible —
practice.solution: **Taproot**, swollen with stored food — like radish, beetroot, turnip. Ginger is the stem-side answer.

practice.q: The **onion bulb** is mainly a modified —
practice.solution: A **bulb** — a compressed underground stem ringed by fleshy scale leaves. Garlic is its cousin.

practice.q: Which part of the plant do we eat in **cauliflower**?
practice.solution: Cauliflower (and broccoli) is a cluster of **undeveloped flower buds**. Cabbage is the leaf; the tomato a fruit.

practice.q: The plant hormone that **ripens fruit** is —
practice.solution: **Ethylene** — a gas; a ripe banana in a closed box ripens the raw fruit beside it. Auxin elongates; ABA stresses.

practice.q: Bending of a shoot **towards light** (phototropism) is caused by —
practice.solution: **Auxin** collects on the shaded side and elongates those cells, so the shoot bends toward light. ABA instead closes stomata under stress.

practice.q: Which hormone promotes **cell division** in plants?
practice.solution: **Cytokinin** — it drives cell division and delays leaf ageing (coconut water is rich in it). Gibberellin stretches stems.

practice.q: The gas **released during photosynthesis** is —
practice.solution: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — the oxygen comes from splitting water. Respiration consumes oxygen instead.

practice.q: Which tissue carries **water** upward from the roots?
practice.solution: **Xylem** = water and minerals, upward; **phloem** = food, both directions. Stomata are pores, not transport tissue.

practice.q: The green pigment essential for photosynthesis is —
practice.solution: **Chlorophyll** in the chloroplasts traps sunlight; it is the reason leaves are green.

practice.q: Which of these is a **monocot** plant?
practice.solution: **Wheat** (and rice, maize, onion) — one seed leaf, parallel veins. Mango, pea and gram are dicots.

practice.q: **Grafting** is a method of —
practice.solution: A stem scion is joined to a rooted stock — no seeds, so the fruit keeps the parent's quality (mango, rose). Layering and cutting are its cousins.

practice.q: The scientific name of **neem** is —
practice.solution: ***Azadirachta indica***. Mango is *Mangifera indica*, banyan *Ficus benghalensis*, rice *Oryza sativa*.

practice.q: In binomial nomenclature, the **first word** of the scientific name denotes the —
practice.solution: Genus first (capitalised), species second (small), both in italics — e.g. *Mangifera indica*. The rule is Linnaeus's.

practice.q: **Ornithology** is the study of —
practice.solution: **Ornithology = birds** (Salim Ali, the birdman of India, was its greatest name here). Entomology is insects.

practice.q: **Ichthyology** is the study of —
practice.solution: **Ichthyology = fishes**. Mycology is fungi; cytology, cells; histology, tissues.

practice.q: **Mycology** is the study of —
practice.solution: **Mycology = fungi** — yeasts, moulds, mushrooms. Virology studies viruses.

practice.q: **Oncology** is the branch of medicine dealing with —
practice.solution: **Oncology = cancer** study and treatment. Cardiology–heart, nephrology–kidney, ophthalmology–eye.

practice.q: **Apiculture** is associated with the rearing of —
practice.solution: **Apiculture = bee-keeping** for honey and wax. Sericulture is silkworms; pisciculture, fish.

practice.q: **Sericulture** is related to —
practice.solution: **Sericulture** rears silkworms on mulberry leaves to produce raw silk.

practice.q: **Pisciculture** deals with —
practice.solution: **Pisciculture = fish culture** (the Blue Revolution). Vermiculture rears earthworms; silviculture, trees.

practice.q: Producers in a food chain trap **10,000 J** of energy. By the **10% law**, the energy at the **third trophic level** is —
practice.solution: 10% each step: 10,000 → **1,000 J** (primary consumers) → **100 J** (secondary carnivores = 3rd level) → 10 J (4th).

practice.q: The **10% law** of energy flow in ecosystems was given by —
practice.solution: **Raymond Lindeman** — only about a tenth of the energy passes to the next trophic level. Odum wrote the classic ecology textbook; Tansley coined 'ecosystem'.

practice.q: In a food chain, **green plants** are called —
practice.solution: **Producers** — they make food by photosynthesis and feed the whole chain; animals are consumers, bacteria and fungi the decomposers.

practice.q: India's **first national park**, set up in 1936, is —
practice.solution: **Jim Corbett** (Uttarakhand, first named Hailey) — 1936. Kaziranga holds rhinos, Gir the lions, Kanha tigers.

practice.q: **Project Tiger** was launched in —
practice.solution: **Project Tiger, 1973**, started from Corbett. The **Chipko movement** is also 1973 — tree-hugging villagers of Uttarakhand.

practice.q: Which bacterium fixes atmospheric **nitrogen in legume root nodules**?
practice.solution: **Rhizobium** lives in pea/gram/bean nodules and turns N₂ into usable compounds — why farmers rotate legumes.

practice.q: The **Green Revolution** in India is associated with —
practice.solution: **M.S. Swaminathan** led India's Green Revolution (high-yield wheat/rice); **Norman Borlaug** is its world father. Kurien = White Revolution (milk).

practice.q: The **White Revolution** (Operation Flood) made India self-sufficient in —
practice.solution: **Milk** — Operation Flood, led by **Verghese Kurien** (Amul). Blue = fish, Yellow = oilseeds, Green = food grain.

practice.q: Who is known as the **'birdman of India'**?
practice.solution: **Salim Ali** — the great ornithologist whose bird surveys and books mapped India's birdlife.

practice.q: **Dolly the sheep** (1996) is famous as the first —
practice.solution: **Dolly** — the first mammal cloned from an adult cell (Roslin Institute, Scotland, 1996), a landmark of biotechnology.

practice.q: A **higher BOD** value of a water sample means the water is —
practice.solution: **Biochemical oxygen demand** — more organic waste feeds more bacteria, which gulp more oxygen: high BOD = dirty water.
